Three dashboards in the style of AI defaults, a report built for Priya's decision, and the weekly dashboard worth automating.

From
Priya Shah, Head of Marketing, Kestrel Lane Records
To
You, data analyst
Subject
Quick summary, Q3 catalogue
Attached

Hi,

Could you send me a quick summary of how our catalogue did in Q3 (July to September)? Next week I have to pick three tracks to pitch to streaming playlist editors1, and I'd like the choice backed by numbers2.

Just the essentials, please.3 The data for all 18 tracks is attached. For reference, Q2 total streams were 1,238,000.4

Thanks,
Priya

  1. The decision. Three tracks, for playlist editors. Everything you send should serve it.
  2. The standard. Each pick needs a number behind it.
  3. The format. A summary she can read in a minute. She decides once, so a one-page report will do. A dashboard is for numbers someone checks every week.
  4. Background. Useful context. Watch which dashboards lead with it.

Ask an AI to make your report "comprehensive" or "more advanced" and it will add things. Each addition makes the answer harder to find.

PartAsk for "comprehensive" and you may getWhat your reader needs

The right-hand column follows today's one-page checklist, Presenting results clearly.

Before you add anything

Keep everything the brief asks for. For anything else, ask two questions:

  1. Would the reader miss it if it were gone?
  2. Does it change the answer?

If both answers are no, leave it out. Before you submit A2 or A3, take one pass through every chart, table and paragraph with these questions.

Ask the AI for less

Before you add or cut a chart, model, package or paragraph, tell me whether the brief asks for it. Keep everything it asks for. For anything else, tell me what it changes in the answer, and if nothing, leave it out.

You can also ask it what a busy reader would misread on your page, then fix that yourself.
